# Methods {#sec-methods}

Every simulated replicate and every real-data split was analysed with the
same twelve methods: two classifiers, each fitted in six ways, a baseline and
five remedies (@tbl-methods). All tuning and all rebalancing use the training
data only; the test set is used once, to score the final predictions.

| Approach | What changes | Cutoff |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline | nothing | 0.5 |
| Over-sampling | positives copied until the classes are 50:50 | 0.5 |
| Under-sampling | negatives dropped until the classes are 50:50 | 0.5 |
| SMOTE | synthetic positives added until the classes are 50:50 | 0.5 |
| Class weights | each positive weighted by #negatives / #positives | 0.5 |
| Threshold moving | nothing; the cutoff is chosen from the training data | Youden |

: The six approaches, each used with both classifiers. {#tbl-methods}

## Classifiers {#sec-classifiers}

Logistic regression models the log-odds of the positive class as a linear
function of the predictors [@islr2, Section 4.3]. We fitted it with the lasso
penalty [@islr2, Section 6.2.2], which maximizes the log-likelihood minus
$\lambda \sum_j |\beta_j|$ and so shrinks small coefficients to exactly zero.
We used `cv.glmnet()` [@friedman2010] with `alpha = 1` and chose $\lambda$ by
10-fold cross-validation on the training set, taking `lambda.min`, the value
with the smallest cross-validated deviance. With five predictors the penalty
does little in the simulation, but it is a sensible choice for the 30
predictors of the real data and it is the model we used in the course labs.
We made one change to the default: the folds are stratified, built separately
within each class, so that every fold contains some positives. With only 10
positives in a training set, purely random folds can leave a fold with none.

A random forest averages many classification trees, each grown on a bootstrap
sample of the training data and, at each split, allowed to choose from only a
random subset of $m$ predictors [@breiman2001; @islr2, Section 8.2.2]. We used
`randomForest()` [@liaw2002] with 200 trees and the default
$m = \lfloor\sqrt{p}\rfloor$, which is 2 of the 5 predictors in the simulation
and 5 of the 30 in the real data. Trees are grown to full depth, the package
default for classification, and the predicted probability is the fraction of
trees that vote for the positive class.

We chose these two classifiers because they sit at opposite ends of the
flexibility scale. In the simulation the logistic model is correctly
specified: apart from the extra noise variable, it is the true model. The
forest makes no assumption about the shape of the boundary and has to learn
the linear boundary from the data.

## The remedies {#sec-remedies}

All the remedies start from the same observation. A model fitted to data with
very few positives, and used with a 0.5 cutoff, rarely calls anything
positive. The remedies differ in where they intervene: in the data, in the
fitting, or only in the decision.

The resampling remedies change the training data so that it has as many
positives as negatives, and then fit the classifier as usual with a 0.5
cutoff [@he2009]. Over-sampling draws positives with replacement and adds
them until the classes are the same size. It adds no new information; each
positive is simply repeated, about $(1 - \pi)/\pi$ times on average.
Under-sampling keeps all the positives and a random subset of negatives of
the same size, so it throws most of the data away: at 1% prevalence and
$n = 1{,}000$ the balanced set has about 20 rows. SMOTE, the synthetic
minority over-sampling technique of @chawla2002, creates new positives
between existing ones. For a randomly chosen positive $a$ it picks one of
its $k = 5$ nearest positive neighbours $b$ and creates a new point
$x_{\text{new}} = x_a + u\,(x_b - x_a)$, with $u$ drawn from a uniform
distribution on $(0, 1)$, so the new point lies somewhere on the line between
$a$ and $b$. We wrote our own short SMOTE function, using `FNN::get.knn()` to
find the neighbours, so that every step was visible to us. SMOTE is still the
most widely used imbalance method, although recent large comparisons find
that its benefit shrinks or disappears for strong classifiers [@elor2022].

Class weights change how much each row counts instead of changing the data.
Each positive gets weight $w = n_0 / n_1$, the number of negatives divided by
the number of positives, so the two classes carry the same total weight
[@he2009]. In `cv.glmnet()` this is the `weights` argument, which multiplies
each row's contribution to the log-likelihood. In `randomForest()` it is the
`classwt` argument, which weights the classes in the Gini criterion used to
choose splits.

For logistic regression there is a clear theoretical expectation for both
resampling and weighting. If positives are kept with probability $r_1$ and
negatives with probability $r_0$, the log-odds in the resampled data equal
the true log-odds plus $\log(r_1/r_0)$; only the intercept changes
[@prentice1979]. Weighting the likelihood has the same effect in
expectation. So when the logistic model is correct, a model fitted to
rebalanced data should differ from the baseline only by a constant added to
every log-odds. Adding a constant does not change the order of the
predictions, so ranking measures such as ROC-AUC and PR-AUC should not change
at all; only the probabilities, and the number of cases above 0.5, should
move. The simulation tests this prediction and also asks what happens when
the model is a forest, when positives are very few, and when the truth is not
logistic. Recent simulation studies in medical prediction reached a similar
expectation and found that these corrections mainly damage calibration
[@vandengoorbergh2022; @carriero2025].

Threshold moving leaves both the data and the model alone. It fits the
baseline model and classifies a case as positive when its predicted
probability exceeds a cutoff $t$ chosen from the training data. A cutoff has
a direct meaning in terms of costs: flagging every case with $\hat p > t$ is
the best decision when a missed positive costs $(1 - t)/t$ times as much as a
false alarm [@elkan2001]. The usual cutoff of 0.5 therefore assumes that the
two mistakes cost the same. We chose $t$ to maximize Youden's index,
sensitivity plus specificity minus one [@youden1950], which is the same as
maximizing balanced accuracy. To avoid choosing the cutoff on predictions the
model has already fitted, we used predictions for training rows that the
model did not use: the out-of-fold predictions saved by `cv.glmnet()` at the
chosen $\lambda$ for the lasso, and the out-of-bag votes for the forest. The
threshold approach therefore needs no extra model fits and never sees the
test set. Because it uses the baseline model, its ROC-AUC and PR-AUC equal
the baseline's by construction, which also served as a check on our code.

## Measuring performance {#sec-metrics}

For each method we predicted $P(y = 1)$ for every test case and compared the
predictions with the true classes. Write TP and FN for positives that were
caught and missed, and TN and FP for negatives that were correctly cleared
and wrongly flagged. The measures below follow @islr2 [Tables 4.6 and 4.7].

Accuracy, $(TP + TN)/(TP + TN + FP + FN)$, is the share of cases classified
correctly. We report it only to show how misleading it is: under strong
imbalance it is close to $1 - \pi$ for any model that rarely flags anything,
and it cannot tell useful models from useless ones [@chicco2020].

Sensitivity (recall), $TP/(TP + FN)$, is the share of positives that are
caught, and specificity, $TN/(TN + FP)$, is the share of negatives that are
correctly cleared. Together they describe the two kinds of error. Precision,
$TP/(TP + FP)$, is the share of flagged cases that really are positive; it
tells an investigator how many false alarms come with each real case. The
$F_1$ score, $2 \cdot \text{precision} \cdot \text{sensitivity} /
(\text{precision} + \text{sensitivity})$, combines precision and sensitivity
into one number, and balanced accuracy, the average of sensitivity and
specificity, is accuracy with both classes given equal weight. All of these
depend on the cutoff, and so on each remedy's choice of operating point.
@chicco2020 discuss how single-number summaries such as $F_1$ and accuracy can
mislead under imbalance, which is why we look at several measures together.

ROC-AUC and PR-AUC do not depend on a cutoff. They summarize how well the
predicted probabilities *rank* positives above negatives over every possible
cutoff. ROC-AUC is the area under the curve of sensitivity against
$1 - \text{specificity}$; it equals the probability that a randomly chosen
positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative, so 0.5 is a
coin flip and 1 is perfect [@islr2, Section 4.4.2]. PR-AUC is the area under
the curve of precision against sensitivity. It concentrates on the rare class
and is more informative than ROC-AUC under imbalance [@saito2015]: a random
ranking gets a PR-AUC equal to the prevalence, so 0.01 at 1% prevalence,
while it always gets an ROC-AUC of 0.5. We computed both with the `ROCR`
package [@sing2005]. These two measures are how we define improving
prediction. A remedy improves prediction if it raises ROC-AUC or PR-AUC; if it
only raises sensitivity, it has moved the operating point.

Calibration is the third aspect of prediction. A model is calibrated if,
among cases given a probability of about 5%, about 5% are positive. We
checked calibration in two simple ways: the mean predicted probability on the
test set, which should match the prevalence, and the Brier score, the mean
of $(\hat p - y)^2$, where lower is better.

Because we know the true probabilities in the simulation, we can also score
the truth itself. The ROC-AUC and PR-AUC of the true probabilities, which we
call the Bayes benchmark, are the best any method can achieve on that test
set (@tbl-sanity), and we report each method's gap to it, in the same way the
course deck compares test error with the irreducible error. For the
cutoff-based measures we cut the true probabilities at the prevalence, which
maximizes sensitivity plus specificity. The usual Bayes classifier cuts at
0.5 and minimizes the overall error rate [@islr2, Section 2.2.3], which under
imbalance is exactly the wrong goal.

## Comparing methods and Monte Carlo error {#sec-mcse}

Because all methods see the same data sets, we compared each remedy with the
baseline replicate by replicate. For replicate $b$ and a measure $M$ we
computed the change $d_b = M_b(\text{remedy}) - M_b(\text{baseline})$, and we
report the mean change $\bar d$ over the $B$ replicates together with its
Monte Carlo standard error [@morris2019],

$$
\text{MCSE}(\bar d) = \frac{\text{sd}(d_1, \dots, d_B)}{\sqrt{B}}.
$$

Pairing removes the variation that comes from the data set itself, so the
MCSE of a change is much smaller than the MCSE of either method's own mean.
Error bars in the figures are $\pm 2$ MCSE. We call a difference a finding
only if it is larger than 2 MCSE *and* at least 0.005, a size that would
matter in practice. With $B = 100$ per setting, or 200 when we pool the two
separation levels, most MCSEs are below 0.002. On the real data the
replicates are the 10 splits, and we report the mean change with its
standard error across splits. The splits share most of their training rows,
so these standard errors are somewhat optimistic, and we treat real-data
differences smaller than about 0.01 with caution.

In total the simulation fitted $1{,}600 \times 12 = 19{,}200$ models and the
real data $10 \times 12 = 120$, plus the EasyEnsemble fits described in
@sec-ensemble.
